list.title: Eosinophilic Asthma:
list.snippet: This is a subtype of asthma where there are increased levels of eosinophils in the lungs and blood.

list.title: Airway Inflammation:
list.snippet: Eosinophils contribute to airway inflammation, which is a key feature of asthma, by releasing substances that damage the airways and cause mucus production.

list.title: Diagnosis:
list.snippet: High eosinophil levels in the blood (typically above 300 cells/µl) or sputum (more than 2-3% of cells) can indicate eosinophilic asthma. However, other conditions can also cause elevated eosinophil counts, so a diagnosis also involves considering medical history and other symptoms.

list.title: Symptoms:
list.snippet: Eosinophilic asthma can cause symptoms similar to other asthma types, such as shortness of breath, wheezing, and coughing. However, it may also be associated with more severe and frequent asthma attacks.

list.title: Treatment:
list.snippet: Treatments for eosinophilic asthma may include inhaled or oral corticosteroids, and in some cases, biologic therapies that target specific pathways involved in eosinophilic inflammation.

text_blocks.snippet: Eosinophils, a type of white blood cell, play a significant role in the inflammation associated with asthma, particularly in a subtype called eosinophilic asthma. These cells, normally involved in fighting infections, can contribute to asthma symptoms when they accumulate in the airways.
snippet_highlighted_words: play a significant role in the inflammation associated with asthma, particularly in a subtype called eosinophilic asthma

list.snippet: Eosinophils are a type of white blood cell that helps the body fight off infections.
They are part of the immune system and can cause inflammation.
In asthma, eosinophils can accumulate in the airways, contributing to inflammation and airway hyperresponsiveness.
Eosinophilic asthma is a subtype of asthma characterized by high levels of eosinophils in the blood, sputum (coughed-up mucus), or lung tissue.
It is often a severe form of asthma, and individuals with this type may experience persistent symptoms despite treatment with inhaled corticosteroids.
Eosinophilic asthma is often associated with Type 2 (Th2) inflammation, which involves the release of certain cytokines (like IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13) that promote eosinophil accumulation.
Eosinophils release various substances, including inflammatory proteins, lipid mediators, and cytokines, that contribute to airway inflammation and remodeling.
These substances can lead to airway narrowing, increased mucus production, and airway hyperresponsiveness, all of which are characteristics of asthma.
While eosinophils play a role in asthma, some research suggests that their contribution may be smaller than previously thought.
Eosinophilic asthma is diagnosed by measuring eosinophil levels in blood, sputum, or through a bronchial biopsy.
Treatment often involves corticosteroids (inhaled or oral) to reduce inflammation and biologics targeting specific pathways involved in eosinophilic inflammation.

Biologics like anti-IL-5 antibodies (e.g., reslizumab, mepolizumab) and anti-IL-5 receptor antibodies (e.g., benralizumab) have shown promise in managing eosinophilic asthma, according to the National Institutes of Health (NIH) | (.gov).

text_blocks.snippet: In summary, eosinophils are key players in eosinophilic asthma, contributing to the inflammation and airway changes associated with this condition. Understanding their role is crucial for developing effective diagnostic and treatment strategies.
